q: most influential female mathematicians of the 19th and 20th centuries
a: Several women made groundbreaking contributions to mathematics in the 19th and 20th centuries despite facing severe institutional discrimination. Sofya Kovalevskaya (1850-1891) was the first woman to earn a doctorate in mathematics (University of Göttingen), the first woman to hold a university chair in mathematics, and made important contributions to analysis and partial differential equations. Her work on the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem remains fundamental. Emmy Noether (1882-1935) revolutionized abstract algebra and theoretical physics. Noether's theorem (1918) shows that every symmetry in physics corresponds to a conservation law — it is a cornerstone of modern physics and was called by Einstein 'the most significant creative mathematical genius thus far produced.' She made fundamental contributions to ring theory, group theory, and algebraic topology. Ada Lovelace (1815-1852) wrote the world's first computer algorithm for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, making her the first computer programmer. Florence Nightingale (1820-1910), primarily known as a nurse, was also a pioneering statistician who used innovative data visualizations (polar area diagrams) to improve military and hospital sanitation. Sophie Germain (1776-1831) made important contributions to number theory and elasticity theory, working under the male pseudonym 'M. LeBlanc.' In the 20th century, Julia Robinson (1919-1985) made crucial contributions to solving Hilbert's Tenth Problem. Katherine Johnson (1918-2020) calculated the trajectories for NASA's Mercury and Apollo missions with extraordinary precision.

q: historical origin of happy birthday song
who wrote the happy birthday song
when was happy birthday song created
a: The song 'Happy Birthday to You' originated in the United States in the late 19th century. The melody was written by sisters Mildred J. Hill (1859-1916), a music teacher, and Patty Smith Hill (1868-1946), a kindergarten educator. They originally composed the tune in 1893 as 'Good Morning to All,' a song for kindergarten classes to start the day. The lyrics were 'Good morning to you, good morning to you, good morning dear children, good morning to all.' The familiar 'Happy Birthday to You' lyrics were first published with the melody in 1912, though the original author of the birthday lyrics is unknown. The song gained widespread popularity in the early 20th century. In 1935, the Hill sisters' copyright was asserted, and the song remained under copyright protection until 2016. For decades, Warner/Chappell Music collected royalties of about $2 million per year for the song's use in films, television, and public performances. In 2013, a class action lawsuit challenged the copyright, and in 2016, a federal judge ruled that the copyright was invalid, placing the song in the public domain. 'Happy Birthday to You' is one of the most recognized songs in the English language and has been translated into dozens of languages.
